extracted.intended_audience: the people/voters of the State of New York (citizens deciding on ratification)
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive political pamphlet (Federalist-style) addressed to state citizens arguing for adoption of the proposed U.S. Constitution and answering objections (e.g., on jury trial, bills of rights, expense, distance, debts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury — scope and constitutional entrenchment
rubrics_metrics.description: The security of liberty is materially concerned only in the trial by jury in criminal cases, which is provided for in the plan; establishing the trial by jury in ALL cases would have been an unpardonable error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt a general constitutional definition making jury trial mandatory in all civil cases: (a) State judicatories vary in common-law jurisdiction so a uniform national rule is impracticable; (b) attempts to fix precise limits would open new sources of opposition; (c) the plan does not abolish jury trial in civil cases and legislative discretion is preferable because social change may render other modes of adjudication preferable in many property cases. Examples/notes: Massachusetts proposition and Pennsylvania minority proposal examined unfavorably; Connecticut and Great Britain show encroachments and variation in practice; see footnote that appellate jurisdiction does not abolish jury (No. 81).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of rights — necessity and danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of rights, in their primitive signification, are stipulations between princes and subjects and have no necessary application to constitutions founded on the power of the people; the proposed Constitution contains various provisions in favor of particular rights and therefore a separate bill of rights is unnecessary and may be dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that: (a) the proposed Constitution already includes many specific safeguards (habeas corpus, prohibition of ex-post-facto laws, prohibition of titles of nobility, jury trial for crimes, treason safeguards); (b) enumerating exceptions (bills of rights) may create 'colorable pretext' for claiming powers by implication (constructive powers) that were not granted; (c) declarations of common law in a constitution are subject to legislative alteration and thus not a constitutional guaranty. Example: specifying 'liberty of the press' might be used to imply a regulatory power exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press — undefinable and secured by public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not a syllable concerning the liberty of the press in some constitutions and no definition of 'liberty of the press' can be given without leaving latitude for evasion; its security must depend on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on a constitutional verbal declaration alone to secure press freedom; emphasize civic culture, public opinion, and institutions. Note legislative tools (e.g., taxation) can affect publications but taxation does not necessarily destroy press liberty (newspapers are taxed in Great Britain yet the press enjoys wide liberty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance to seat of government — not fatal to accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection that the national seat will be too remote to permit constituents to judge representatives is ill-founded: citizens already rely on public prints, correspondences, and intermediaries to judge state legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter the distance objection by showing: (a) the same informational channels exist for national government as for state governments; (b) state executives and legislatures will act as sentinels over national officers and will communicate abuses; (c) citizens near the seat and the public papers will provide timely information. Use this to rebut claims that remoteness implies unaccountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debts due to the United States — omission is not relinquishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of provision respecting the debts due to the United States in the proposed Constitution does not amount to a tacit relinquishment of those debts or a scheme to screen public defaulters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke established political-law doctrine: 'States neither lose any of their rights, nor are discharged from any of their obligations, by a change in the form of their civil government.' Use this legal principle to refute populist claims that omission equals forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense objection — increased cost is not decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: If adoption of the proposed government would occasion a considerable increase of expense, that is an objection which ought to have no weight against the plan; many supposed new expenses are transfers or counterbalanced by savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze sources of expense and savings: (a) many federal officers merely replace state officers (e.g., revenue collectors); (b) principal departments already exist under current system; (c) the President will transact business now occupying Congress, shortening sessions and saving expense; (d) state legislatures will no longer spend much time on federal business, reducing their sessions and saving costs; (e) support of federal judges is an extra expense but not materially consequential. Use arithmetic/organizational argument to rebut fear of excessive cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union's benefits — restraints on factions and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional securities to republican government, liberty, and property from adopting the plan consist chiefly in restraints on local factions and insurrections, diminution of foreign intrigue, prevention of extensive military establishments, express guaranty of a republican form, exclusion of titles of nobility, and precautions against state practices that have undermined property and credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing objections, emphasize these systemic benefits as outweighing imperfections. Spell out each protective function (restraint on local ambition, foreign intrigue prevention, military establishment avoidance, guarantee of republican government, exclusion of nobility, and protection of property/credit) as compensating advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: General genius of government matters more than particular provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The general genius of a government is all that can be substantially relied upon for permanent effects; particular provisions, though not useless, have far less virtue and efficacy than commonly ascribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to argue against overreliance on enumerated guarantees (e.g., a separate bill of rights). Encourage evaluation of the constitution's overall character and mechanisms rather than fixation on isolated textual assurances.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proposed Constitution functions as a bill of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution, if adopted, will be the bill of rights of the Union: it comprehends structural political privileges and many immunities and modes of proceeding relative to personal and private concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the order or form of declaring rights is immaterial if the instrument contains the substantive protections; thus objections based on the absence of a prefixed bill of rights are largely verbal or nominal and not substantive. Point to specific clauses (habeas corpus, ex-post-facto prohibition, jury trial for crimes, treason rules, no titles of nobility) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting imperfect systems for perfection is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessions that the plan is not absolutely perfect have been exaggerated by opponents; the plea 'Why not amend and make perfect before adopting?' is only plausible and cannot justify rejecting a necessary and superior system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel citizens to judge by practical necessity and comparative fitness: adoption of an imperfect but necessary and superior constitution is preferable to waiting for unattainable perfection. Warn against obstinate party adherence, passions, and partial interests leading to improper rejection of a plan needed for the nation's existence.
